context: Francesco Petrarca (1304–1374), the Italian poet often called the father of humanism, wrote the Secret as an imagined conversation about his own life. Here he admits what many feel: knowing a fault is not the same as being free of it.
prompt: Which habit have you tried hardest to break?

text: For human beings are not so constituted that they can live without expansion.
source: Margaret Fuller, Woman in the Nineteenth Century
context: Margaret Fuller (1810–1850), the only woman in the Transcendentalist inner circle, argued that every person, man or woman, needs room to grow.
prompt: Where do you need more room to grow?

text: We would have every path laid open to Woman as freely as to Man.
source: Margaret Fuller, Woman in the Nineteenth Century
context: Fuller's book (1845) was one of the first major feminist works in the United States.
prompt: Which paths are still less open to some people than to others?

text: This self-dependence, which was honored in me, is deprecated as a fault in most women.
source: Margaret Fuller, Woman in the Nineteenth Century
context: Fuller noticed that independence was praised in her only because she was an exception. The same quality was criticised in other women.
prompt: Which quality is praised in some people and criticised in others?

text: If I can stop one heart from breaking, / I shall not live in vain; …
context: Emily Dickinson (1830–1886) published almost nothing in her lifetime; her poems appeared after her death. Here a life's worth is measured by the small kindness of easing one heart.
prompt: Whose heart could you ease in the days ahead?

text: Success is counted sweetest / By those who ne'er succeed.
context: Those who never win understand best what winning means. Longing sharpens our sense of value.
prompt: What do you value more because you don't have it?

text: Much madness is divinest sense / To a discerning eye; …
context: Dickinson goes on to say that the majority decides what counts as sane, and punishes those who disagree. Sometimes what looks mad is the clearest sight.
prompt: What 'madness' of yours might actually be sense?

text: True eloquence consists in saying all that should be, not all that could be said.
context: Good speaking is mostly a matter of knowing what to leave out.
prompt: What could you leave unsaid next time?
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Few things are impossible in themselves; application to make them succeed fails us more often than the means.
context: We blame impossibility when the real problem is that we didn't keep at it.
prompt: What did you call impossible that was really a lack of persistence?
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Self-love is the greatest of flatterers.
context: No one flatters us as well as we flatter ourselves. La Rochefoucauld built his whole book on this insight.
prompt: What flattering story do you tell yourself?
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: Pride will not owe, self-love will not pay.
context: Pride hates being in someone's debt, and self-love hates repaying it. Gratitude is harder than it looks.
prompt: Whom do you owe thanks to but haven't said it?
translation: J. W. Willis Bund and J. Hain Friswell (1871)

text: To divert myself from a troublesome fancy, 'tis but to run to my books; …
source: Michel de Montaigne, Essays, III.3 'Of Three Commerces'
context: Montaigne describes his three companions: friends, women, and books. Books, he says, are always there and never complain.
prompt: Where do you go to clear a troubled mind?
translation: Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt (1877)

text: …if I am not much deceived, I am the same within that I am without.
source: Michel de Montaigne, Essays, III.2 'Of Repentance'
context: Montaigne valued being the same person in private as in public. Integrity means no gap between the two.
prompt: How different are you in private and in public?
translation: Charles Cotton, ed. W. C. Hazlitt (1877)

text: For every thing you have missed, you have gained something else; and for every thing you gain, you lose something.
context: Emerson's 'law of compensation': life balances itself. Every gain has a cost, and every loss a hidden gift.
prompt: What did you gain from something you missed?

text: Every sweet hath its sour; every evil its good.
context: Six words that echo Taoist and Stoic ideas: nothing is purely good or bad.
prompt: What is the sour in your sweet, and the good in your evil?

text: All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts. If a man speaks or acts with an evil thought, pain follows him, as the wheel follows the foot of the ox that draws the carriage.
context: The first verse of the Dhammapada, a collection of sayings attributed to the Buddha. It places the mind at the root of experience: the way we habitually think shapes who we become.
prompt: Which thought have you repeated so often that it now feels like a fact?

text: For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love, this is an old rule.
context: Presented not as a new commandment but as an 'old rule', a law of how things work. Answering hostility with hostility only feeds the cycle.
prompt: Is there a resentment you are keeping alive by feeding it?

text: As a solid rock is not shaken by the wind, wise people falter not amidst blame and praise.
context: Praise and blame are counted among the 'eight worldly winds' in Buddhist teaching, along with gain and loss, fame and disrepute, pleasure and pain. The wise remain steady in all of them.
prompt: How much of your mood today depends on what others think of you?

text: If one man conquer in battle a thousand times thousand men, and if another conquer himself, he is the greatest of conquerors.
context: From the chapter on 'thousands'. Mastery of one's own mind is placed above any outward victory.
prompt: What small inner victory would matter most today?

text: Let no man think lightly of evil, saying in his heart, It will not come near me. Even by the falling of water-drops a water-pot is filled; the fool becomes full of evil, even if he gather it little by little.
context: The verse that follows makes the same point about good. Character is built drop by drop, through small acts we hardly notice.
prompt: What small habit is slowly filling your pot?

text: The world does not know that we must all come to an end here;—but those who know it, their quarrels cease at once.
context: The Dhammapada, a collection of the Buddha's sayings, notes that we quarrel as if we had forever. Remembering that every life ends puts most arguments in proportion.
prompt: Which disagreement would fade if you remembered how short life is?

text: By rousing himself, by earnestness, by restraint and control, the wise man may make for himself an island which no flood can overwhelm.
context: The 'flood' in Buddhist imagery is the rush of craving and confusion. Steady effort builds an island where the mind can stand.
prompt: What practice could be your island?

text: As a fletcher makes straight his arrow, a wise man makes straight his trembling and unsteady thought, which is difficult to guard, difficult to hold back.
context: A fletcher straightens arrows by patient heating and bending. The mind can be trained the same way.
prompt: Where is your thinking bent today, and how might you straighten it?

text: It is good to tame the mind, which is difficult to hold in and flighty, rushing wherever it likes; a tamed mind brings happiness.
context: The Buddha compares the untrained mind to something wild, rushing wherever it likes. Taming it is not about force but steadiness, and a steady mind brings ease.
prompt: Where did your mind rush off to today?

text: Not a mother, not a father will do so much, nor any other relative; a well-directed mind will do us greater service.
context: The Dhammapada makes a bold claim: even our parents cannot do as much for us as a well-trained mind. Our way of thinking goes everywhere with us.
prompt: What direction would you like to give your mind today?

text: Not the perversities of others, not their sins of commission or omission, but his own misdeeds and negligences should a sage take notice of.
context: A wise person pays attention to their own faults and failures, not to other people's. It is far easier to count others' mistakes than to notice our own.
prompt: What would you notice if you looked at your own day the way you look at others'?

text: Like a beautiful flower, full of colour, but without scent, are the fine but fruitless words of him who does not act accordingly.
context: Beautiful words without matching action are like a flower with no scent: lovely to look at, but empty.
prompt: Which of your words are still waiting for their deeds?

text: Long is the night to him who is awake; long is a mile to him who is tired; long is life to the foolish who do not know the true law.
context: Three images of time stretching: a sleepless night, a mile walked when tired, and a life lived without understanding. Each feels long because something is missing.
prompt: What makes your days feel long, and what makes them feel full?

text: The fool who knows his foolishness, is wise at least so far. But a fool who thinks himself wise, he is called a fool indeed.
context: The Dhammapada's view of wisdom is humble: a fool who knows he is a fool is already a little wise. The real danger is believing we understand when we do not.
prompt: Where might you be the fool who thinks himself wise?

text: Well-makers lead the water wherever they like; fletchers bend the arrow; carpenters bend a log of wood; wise people fashion themselves.
context: Every craftsman shapes a material: water, arrows, wood. The Dhammapada says the wise treat their own character the same way, as something to be shaped with skill.
prompt: What part of yourself are you shaping right now?

text: Wise people, after they have listened to the laws, become serene, like a deep, smooth, and still lake.
context: The Dhammapada says that teaching truly understood does not stir us up but settles us, like a deep lake whose surface has gone still.
prompt: What would help your mind become a little more still today?

text: Even though a speech be a thousand words, but made up of senseless words, one word of sense is better, which if a man hears, he becomes quiet.
context: The Dhammapada values words by their effect, not their number. One sentence that brings calm and clarity is worth more than a thousand empty ones.
prompt: What one word of sense do you need to hear, or to say?

text: All men tremble at punishment, all men fear death; remember that you are like them, and do not kill, nor cause slaughter.
context: The ethic of non-harm rests on a simple act of imagination: others fear pain and death just as we do.
prompt: Whose fear could you understand better by putting yourself in their place?

text: Do not speak harshly to anybody; those who are spoken to will answer you in the same way. Angry speech is painful, blows for blows will touch you.
context: The Dhammapada's advice on speech is practical before it is moral: harsh words come back to the speaker, like a blow returned.
prompt: What tone have you been using with the people around you?

text: Let each man direct himself first to what is proper, then let him teach others; thus a wise man will not suffer.
context: The Dhammapada puts the order plainly: first set yourself on the right course, then guide others. Advice from someone who does not live it carries little weight.
prompt: What advice you often give could you take yourself?

text: Self is the lord of self, who else could be the lord? With self well subdued, a man finds a lord such as few can find.
context: Self-reliance is at the heart of the Buddha's teaching: no one else can master our mind for us. Whoever learns to govern themselves has found a rare kind of guide.
prompt: Where are you waiting for someone else to change what only you can?

text: By oneself the evil is done, by oneself one suffers; by oneself evil is left undone, by oneself one is purified. Purity and impurity belong to oneself, no one can purify another.
context: The Dhammapada makes responsibility personal: no one can do our wrongs for us, and no one can make us better in our place. The work is ours alone.
prompt: What is yours alone to take responsibility for?

text: Let us live happily then, not hating those who hate us! among men who hate us let us dwell free from hatred!
context: From the chapter on happiness. Happiness here is not the absence of hostility, but freedom from returning it.
prompt: What would it feel like to live free from hatred, even toward one person?

text: Victory breeds hatred, for the conquered is unhappy. He who has given up both victory and defeat, he, the contented, is happy.
context: The Dhammapada notes that every victory creates a loser, and the loser's bitterness. Real contentment lies outside the game of winning and losing.
prompt: Where are you trying to win when you could simply let go?

text: Health is the greatest of gifts, contentedness the best riches; trust is the best of relationships, Nirvana the highest happiness.
context: A list of what truly counts as wealth. Nirvana is the Buddhist name for the final peace beyond craving.
prompt: By this measure, how rich are you today?

text: He who holds back rising anger like a rolling chariot, him I call a real driver; other people are but holding the reins.
context: Anger is pictured as a runaway chariot. The real driver is the one who can stop it.
prompt: When did you last hold back anger, and how did it feel afterwards?

text: Let a man overcome anger by love, let him overcome evil by good; let him overcome the greedy by liberality, the liar by truth!
context: The Dhammapada proposes answering each harm with its opposite: anger with love, greed with generosity, lies with truth. Answering in kind only feeds the cycle.
prompt: Which opposite does a situation in your life call for?

text: Let a wise man blow off the impurities of his self, as a smith blows off the impurities of silver one by one, little by little, and from time to time.
context: Refining silver takes patient, repeated work, removing impurities a little at a time. The Dhammapada says character is refined the same way, never all at once.
prompt: What small impurity could you work on, little by little?

text: A man is not learned because he talks much; he who is patient, free from hatred and fear, he is called learned.
context: Real learning shows in character (patience, freedom from fear and hatred), not in how much one talks.
prompt: Where could you speak less and understand more?

text: If by leaving a small pleasure one sees a great pleasure, let a wise man leave the small pleasure, and look to the great.
context: A simple trade from the Dhammapada: give up a small pleasure now when it leads to a greater and more lasting one. Most self-discipline comes down to this choice.
prompt: What small pleasure stands between you and a greater one?

text: As rain does not break through a well-thatched house, passion will not break through a well-reflecting mind.
context: A well-built roof keeps out the storm; a mind used to reflecting keeps out sudden passions.
prompt: What keeps your mind 'well-thatched' on stormy days?

text: If a man does what is good, let him do it again; let him delight in it: happiness is the outcome of good.
context: Good habits are built by repeating good acts, and the Buddha adds that we should enjoy them, not just endure them.
prompt: Which good thing could you do again today?

text: Bad deeds, and deeds hurtful to ourselves, are easy to do; what is beneficial and good, that is very difficult to do.
context: The easy road and the good road are rarely the same. Knowing this in advance makes the effort less surprising.
prompt: What good thing are you avoiding because it is hard?

text: There never was, there never will be, nor is there now, a man who is always blamed, or a man who is always praised.
context: Everyone gets both praise and blame. Taking either too seriously makes us its prisoner.
prompt: Whose praise or blame matters too much to you?

text: The wise who control their body, who control their tongue, the wise who control their mind, are indeed well controlled.
context: Body, speech, and mind: the three places where self-control is practised in Buddhist ethics.
prompt: Which of the three, body, tongue, or mind, is hardest for you to control?

text: 'Here I shall dwell in the rain, here in winter and summer,' thus the fool meditates, and does not think of his death.
context: We make plans as if we will live forever. The Buddha doesn't forbid plans; he asks us to remember they are temporary.
prompt: Which of your plans assumes you have unlimited time?

text: Good people shine from afar, like the snowy mountains; bad people are not seen, like arrows shot by night.
context: Goodness is visible from a distance, like snow on a peak. Harm works in the dark.
prompt: Who shines from afar in your life?

text: Earnest among the thoughtless, awake among the sleepers, the wise man advances like a racer, leaving behind the hack.
context: 'Earnestness' translates appamada: being alert and wholehearted. It is what moves us forward while others drift.
prompt: Where are you sleepwalking instead of being awake?

text: 'All created things perish,' he who knows and sees this becomes passive in pain; this is the way to purity.
context: Seeing that everything changes and ends is, for the Buddha, the beginning of peace. 'Passive' here means no longer thrown around by pain.
prompt: What would hurt less if you remembered that it will pass?

text: Fools follow after vanity, men of evil wisdom. The wise man keeps earnestness as his best jewel.
context: Vanity chases appearances; wisdom treasures steady, wholehearted effort.
prompt: What vanity is drawing your attention away from what matters?

text: As the bee collects nectar and departs without injuring the flower, or its colour or scent, so let a sage dwell in his village.
context: A beautiful picture of living lightly: take what you need from the world and leave it unharmed.
prompt: Where could you take what you need without harming anything?

text: If you see an intelligent man who tells you where true treasures are to be found, who shows what is to be avoided, and administers reproofs, follow that wise man; it will be better, not worse, for those who follow him.
context: Someone who honestly points out our faults is giving us treasure. The Buddha advises seeking such people out.
prompt: Who tells you the truth about yourself, and do you listen?

text: The fault of others is easily perceived, but that of oneself is difficult to perceive; a man winnows his neighbour's faults like chaff, but his own fault he hides, as a cheat hides the bad die from the gambler.
context: We sift other people's faults carefully and hide our own. An old observation that psychology has since confirmed.
prompt: Which of your own faults are you hiding from yourself?

text: Let no one forget his own duty for the sake of another's, however great; let a man, after he has discerned his own duty, be always attentive to his duty.
context: Helping others matters, but not at the cost of neglecting our own path. Find your task and give it attention.
prompt: Have you neglected your own path while helping others with theirs?

text: And he who lives a hundred years, idle and weak, a life of one day is better if a man has attained firm strength.
context: A short life lived with energy is worth more than a long one lived half-asleep.
prompt: What would one fully lived day look like for you?

text: A man who has learnt little, grows old like an ox; his flesh grows, but his knowledge does not grow.
context: Getting older doesn't make us wiser on its own. Without learning, we only grow in body.
prompt: What have you learned recently that made you grow?

text: There is no fire like passion, there is no shark like hatred, there is no snare like folly, there is no torrent like greed.
context: Four vivid images for the forces that harm us from inside.
prompt: Which of the four, passion, hatred, folly, or greed, catches you most often?

text: If a traveller does not meet with one who is his better, or his equal, let him firmly keep to his solitary journey; there is no companionship with a fool.
context: Better to walk alone than in company that pulls you down.
prompt: Which company lifts you up, and which pulls you down?

text: Then thus, ask as I may, I can discover no chariot. Chariot is a mere empty sound.
source: The Questions of King Milinda, Book II
context: The monk Nagasena asks a Greek king in India whether the chariot is its pole, wheels, or axle. It is none of them alone: 'chariot' is just a name for parts working together. So too, he says, is the self.
prompt: If you are not any one of your parts, what are you?

text: Let the wise man guard his thoughts, for they are difficult to perceive, very artful, and they rush wherever they list: thoughts well guarded bring happiness.
context: Thoughts arrive quickly and quietly, and they pull us wherever they like. The Buddha's advice is not to stop them, but to watch over them, the way you would guard a door.
prompt: Which thought has been rushing wherever it likes today?

text: Let no man think lightly of good, saying in his heart, It will not come nigh unto me. Even by the falling of water-drops a water-pot is filled; the wise man becomes full of good, even if he gather it little by little.
context: Goodness is built drop by drop. No single kind act seems to matter much, but small acts repeated fill a life, just as small faults do.
prompt: What small good thing could you add to the pot today?

text: Let a man leave anger, let him forsake pride, let him overcome all bondage! No sufferings befall the man who is not attached to name and form, and who calls nothing his own.
context: Anger and pride both hold on to something: a grievance, an image of ourselves. The Buddha's advice is to loosen the grip; what we don't cling to can't hurt us in the same way.
prompt: What are you holding on to that keeps your anger going?

text: This mind of mine went formerly wandering about as it liked, as it listed, as it pleased; but I shall now hold it in thoroughly, as the rider who holds the hook holds in the furious elephant.
context: Early Buddhist texts often picture the untrained mind as a wild elephant. The rider doesn't fight it; with steady attention, he learns to guide it.
prompt: Where did your mind wander today, and how did you bring it back?

text:
Finally, this is better, that one do
His own task as he may, even though he fail,
Than take tasks not his own, though they seem good.
context: Better to walk your own path imperfectly than someone else's perfectly. In the Gita this is dharma: the duty that fits who you are.
prompt: Whose path are you trying to walk instead of your own?

context: Krishna admits that the human heart is hard to control and restless, but says it can be trained by habit. Arjuna had complained it was as hard to hold as the wind.
prompt: What small daily practice could steady your mind?

text:
And like the ocean, day by day receiving
Floods from all lands, which never overflows
Its boundary-line not leaping, and not leaving,
Fed by the rivers, but unswelled by those;—
So is the perfect one!
context: The ocean receives rivers from every land and never overflows. A wise person is like that: pleasures and temptations flow in without disturbing their calm.
prompt: What keeps pouring into your days, and how do you stay steady?

text: The good is one thing, the pleasant another; these two, having different objects, chain a man. It is well with him who clings to the good; he who chooses the pleasant, misses his end.
context: In the Katha Upanishad, Death himself teaches a young seeker called Nachiketas. His first lesson: what feels good now and what is good are often different roads.
prompt: Where are you choosing the pleasant over the good?
translation: F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 15 (1884)

text: Know the Self to be sitting in the chariot, the body to be the chariot, the intellect (buddhi) the charioteer, and the mind the reins.
context: An image close to Plato's charioteer, from a different culture. The body is the vehicle, the mind holds the reins, and the self sits inside. So who is steering?
prompt: Who is really holding the reins in your life right now?
translation: F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 15 (1884)

text: Rise, awake! having obtained your boons, understand them! The sharp edge of a razor is difficult to pass over; thus the wise say the path (to the Self) is hard.
context: A call to wake up and understand the gifts we have been given. The path to knowing yourself is as narrow as a razor's edge. Somerset Maugham took the title of his novel The Razor's Edge from this verse.
prompt: What gift or chance have you received but not yet used?
translation: F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 15 (1884)

text: And he who beholds all beings in the Self, and the Self in all beings, he never turns away from it. When to a man who understands, the Self has become all things, what sorrow, what trouble can there be to him who once beheld that unity?
context: Someone who sees all beings as part of themselves, and themselves in all beings, can't turn away from anyone, and has nothing left to fear or grieve. The Upanishads teach that the deepest self is one with everything.
prompt: How would you treat the people around you if you saw them as part of yourself?
translation: F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 1 (1879)

text: And here they say that a person consists of desires. And as is his desire, so is his will; and as is his will, so is his deed; and whatever deed he does, that he will reap.
context: A chain from the inside out: desire shapes will, will shapes action, and action shapes what comes back to us. It is one of the earliest statements of the idea of karma.
prompt: Which of your desires is quietly shaping your actions?
translation: F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 15 (1884)

text: Your business is with action alone; not by any means with fruit. Let not the fruit of action be your motive to action. Let not your attachment be fixed on inaction.
context: The Gita is a dialogue between Prince Arjuna and the god Krishna before a great battle. Its central teaching: do your work well and let go of the outcome, without using that as an excuse to do nothing.
prompt: What would you do differently if you stopped worrying about the result?
translation: Kashinath Trimbak Telang, Sacred Books of the East vol. 8 (1882), lightly modernised

text: He whose heart is not agitated in the midst of calamities, who has no longing for pleasures, and from whom the feelings of affection, fear, and wrath have departed, is called a sage of steady mind.
context: Krishna's portrait of a steady mind: not cold, but no longer thrown around by every gain and loss.
prompt: What knocks you off balance most easily?
translation: Kashinath Trimbak Telang, Sacred Books of the East vol. 8 (1882), lightly modernised

text: The man who ponders over objects of sense forms an attachment to them; from that attachment is produced desire; and from desire anger is produced; from anger results want of discrimination; from want of discrimination, confusion of the memory; from confusion of the memory, loss of reason; and in consequence of loss of reason, he is utterly ruined.
context: Dwelling on something leads to wanting it; wanting leads to anger when we don't get it; anger clouds judgment; and lost judgment ruins us. The easiest place to break the chain is the first link.
prompt: Which thought do you keep returning to that might be the first link in a chain?
translation: Kashinath Trimbak Telang, Sacred Books of the East vol. 8 (1882), lightly modernised

text: A man should elevate his self by his self; he should not debase his self, for even a man's own self is his friend, a man's own self is also his enemy.
context: No one else can raise us up or pull us down as effectively as we can. Each of us is both our best ally and our worst opponent.
prompt: Were you your own friend or your own enemy today?
translation: Kashinath Trimbak Telang, Sacred Books of the East vol. 8 (1882), lightly modernised

text: Devotion is not his, O Arjuna! who eats too much, nor his who eats not at all; not his who is addicted to too much sleep, nor his who is ever awake.
context: Like the Buddha's 'middle way' and Aristotle's 'mean', the Gita warns against extremes in both directions. Spiritual practice starts with ordinary balance.
prompt: Where in your daily life are you living at an extreme?
translation: Kashinath Trimbak Telang, Sacred Books of the East vol. 8 (1882), lightly modernised

text: Two birds, inseparable friends, cling to the same tree. One of them eats the sweet fruit, the other looks on without eating.
context: One bird is the part of us that tastes, wants, and suffers; the other is the quiet witness within. Both live on the same tree.
prompt: Can you watch your own wanting today without acting on it?
translation: F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 15 (1884)

text: Essentially man is not a slave either of himself or of the world; but he is a lover.
source: Rabindranath Tagore, Sadhana, 'The Relation of the Individual to the Universe'
context: Tagore (1861–1941), the first non-European Nobel laureate in literature, gave these lectures on the Upanishads at Harvard. For him, our deepest relation to the world is love, not use.
prompt: Do you relate to your work and world more as a servant or as a lover?

text: Man's poverty is abysmal, his wants are endless till he becomes truly conscious of his soul.
context: No amount of possessions fills a gap that is really about meaning. Tagore says our wants only settle when we know what we are.
prompt: What are you trying to fill with things that things can't fill?

text: Man's cry is to reach his fullest expression.
context: Behind much of our restlessness, Tagore hears one longing: to become fully who we are.
prompt: Which part of you is still waiting to be expressed?

text: We gain our freedom when we attain our truest nature.
source: Rabindranath Tagore, Sadhana, 'The Problem of Self'
context: Freedom, for Tagore, isn't doing whatever we like. It is becoming what we most deeply are.
prompt: When do you feel most like yourself?

text: …when a man loves, giving becomes a matter of joy to him, like the tree's surrender of the ripe fruit.
source: Rabindranath Tagore, Sadhana, 'The Problem of Self'
context: A tree does not feel it loses anything when its fruit falls. When we love, giving stops feeling like a sacrifice.
prompt: Where does giving feel easy for you, and where does it feel like loss?

text: …we do cross the infinite at every step, and meet the eternal in every second.
context: Tagore rejects the idea that the infinite is far away. It is present in every ordinary step and moment.
prompt: What ordinary moment today could you treat as extraordinary?

text: Good and evil have an equal share in moulding character, and in some instances misery is a greater teacher than happiness.
context: Vivekananda (1863–1902) brought Vedanta to Western audiences in the 1890s, lecturing in English. Here he says that hard times shape us as much as good ones.
prompt: What did a difficult time teach you that a good one couldn't?

text: Work incessantly, but be not attached to it.
source: Swami Vivekananda, Karma-Yoga, ch. 3 'The Secret of Work'
context: His summary of the Gita's teaching for modern working life: give full effort, but don't let the work own you.
prompt: Does your work belong to you, or do you belong to it?

text: Attachment comes only where we expect a return.
source: Swami Vivekananda, Karma-Yoga, ch. 3 'The Secret of Work'
context: We get tangled up in what we do when we keep an invisible bill for it. Giving without expecting frees us.
prompt: What are you doing mainly for what you hope to get back?

text: In helping the world we really help ourselves.
source: Swami Vivekananda, Karma-Yoga, ch. 5 'We Help Ourselves, Not the World'
context: Vivekananda suggests that the world doesn't need us as much as we need to help it. Service shapes the one who serves.
prompt: How has helping someone changed you?

text: It is not the receiver that is blessed, but it is the giver.
source: Swami Vivekananda, Karma-Yoga, ch. 5 'We Help Ourselves, Not the World'
context: Rather than feeling superior when we give, we should feel grateful for the chance to do it.
prompt: Who gave you the chance to be generous recently?

text: Life is given to us, we earn it by giving it.
context: Tagore wrote Stray Birds (1916) in English: short sayings, many inspired by Japanese haiku. Here he suggests that a life becomes truly ours through what we give.
prompt: What are you giving that makes your life your own?

text: Death's stamp gives value to the coin of life; making it possible to buy with life what is truly precious.
context: Because life ends, every hour has value, like a coin stamped by a mint. Mortality is what makes our choices matter.
prompt: What would you 'buy' with your remaining time if you saw it as precious?

text: Death belongs to life as birth does. The walk is in the raising of the foot as in the laying of it down.
context: Walking needs both lifting and placing the foot. Life, Tagore says, needs both birth and death.
prompt: How would you live differently if you saw death as part of the walk?

text: He who wants to do good knocks at the gate; he who loves finds the gate open.
context: Trying hard to be good can feel like knocking on a closed door. Love opens it without effort.
prompt: Where are you knocking when you could simply love?

text: We live in this world when we love it.
context: We can exist in the world without really living in it. Love is what makes us present.
prompt: What part of your world have you stopped loving?

text: Rest belongs to the work as the eyelids to the eyes.
context: Eyes need eyelids to keep working; work needs rest. Rest is not the enemy of effort but part of it.
prompt: When did you last rest as part of your work, not as an escape from it?

text: If you shut your door to all errors truth will be shut out.
context: Fear of being wrong closes us to learning. Truth comes in through the same door as mistakes.
prompt: What mistake are you afraid to risk?

text: The small truth has words that are clear; the great truth has great silence.
context: Facts can be stated easily. The deepest truths, about love, death, and meaning, are harder to put into words.
prompt: What do you know deeply but can't explain?

text: We come nearest to the great when we are great in humility.
context: True greatness is not reached by pride but by humility.
prompt: Where could humility bring you closer to what you admire?

text: The waterfall sings, 'I find my song, when I find my freedom.'
context: Water held back is silent; released, it sings. Our own voice appears when we are free to be ourselves.
prompt: What would your 'song' be if you felt completely free?

text: What you are you do not see, what you see is your shadow.
context: We see only the outline we cast on the world, not our full self.
prompt: What part of you do others see that you don't?

text: Do not insult your friend by lending him merits from your own pocket.
context: Praising a friend for qualities they don't have, or that are really ours, is a quiet insult. Real friendship sees people as they are.
prompt: Do you see your friends as they are, or as you'd like them to be?

text: To be outspoken is easy when you do not wait to speak the complete truth.
context: Blunt speech can pass for honesty. The whole truth takes patience and care.
prompt: When did your bluntness leave out part of the truth?

text: Life has become richer by the love that has been lost.
context: Lost love leaves sorrow, but also depth. Tagore sees it as a gift rather than only a wound.
prompt: How has a love you lost enriched your life?

text: Kicks only raise dust and not crops from the earth.
context: Force and anger make noise but produce nothing. Growth needs patient work.
prompt: Where are you kicking when you should be planting?

text: His freedom and fulfilment is in love, which is another name for perfect comprehension.
source: Rabindranath Tagore, Sadhana, 'The Relation of the Individual to the Universe'
context: For Tagore, to love something fully is to understand it fully, and that is where we find freedom.
prompt: What do you understand best because you love it?

text: Whatever a great man does, that other men also do. And people follow whatever he receives as authority.
context: Krishna reminds Arjuna that leaders set an example whether they mean to or not. Others copy what we do more than what we say.
prompt: Who is copying your example without your noticing?

text: For nobody ever remains even for an instant without performing some action …
context: Even doing nothing is a kind of action. The question is not whether to act, but how.
prompt: What are you 'doing' by not doing anything?

text: He who is alike to friend and foe, as also in honour and dishonour, who is alike in cold and heat, pleasure and pain, who is free from attachments, to whom praise and blame are alike, who is taciturn, and contented with anything whatever …
context: Krishna's portrait of a steady person: not cold, but no longer thrown around by every change in fortune or opinion.
prompt: Which of these pairs throws you off balance most?

text: Misery comes through attachment, not through work.
context: Hard work rarely makes us miserable on its own. Clinging to its results does.
prompt: Is it the work, or your attachment to it, that tires you?

text: Everything that you do under compulsion goes to build up attachment.
context: What we do freely leaves us free; what we do because we feel we must binds us.
prompt: What are you doing only because you feel you must?

text: He works best who works without any motive, neither for money, nor for fame, nor for anything else; …
context: Work done for its own sake is often the best work, because nothing distracts from it.
prompt: What would you work on if no one paid or praised you?

text: Let us do good because it is good to do good; …
context: Doing good for a reward turns kindness into a trade. Vivekananda asks us to do it for its own sake.
prompt: What good thing would you do even if no one ever knew?

text: No one was ever really taught by another; each of us has to teach himself.
context: Teachers can point the way, but understanding is something we do ourselves.
prompt: What lesson have you had to teach yourself?

text: The true prevails, not the untrue; …
context: In its Sanskrit form, satyameva jayate, this line is India's national motto, written beneath the national emblem.
prompt: Where have you seen truth win in the end?

text: The highest excellence is like that of water. The excellence of water appears in its benefiting all things, and in its occupying, without striving to the contrary, the low place which all men dislike.
context: Water is Taoism's favourite teacher: it nourishes everything, never fights, and settles where nobody else wants to be.
prompt: Where could you be more like water today?

text: He who knows other men is discerning; he who knows himself is intelligent. He who overcomes others is strong; he who overcomes himself is mighty. He who is satisfied with his lot is rich; he who goes on acting with energy has a firm will.
context: In four short contrasts, Laozi weighs outer success against inner achievement: knowing others against knowing yourself, beating others against mastering yourself.
prompt: Which kind of strength are you building: over others, or over yourself?

text: The thirty spokes unite in the one nave; but it is on the empty space for the axle, that the use of the wheel depends. Clay is fashioned into vessels; but it is on their empty hollowness, that their use depends. The door and windows are cut out from the walls to form an apartment; but it is on the empty space within, that its use depends.
context: A wheel works because of the empty hole in its centre, a bowl because of its hollow, a room because of its open space. What is empty is what makes things useful.
prompt: Where could some emptiness make your life more useful, not less?

text: The tree which fills the arms grew from the tiniest sprout; the tower of nine storeys rose from a small heap of earth; the journey of a thousand li commenced with a single step.
context: The source of the saying 'a journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step'. A li is a traditional Chinese measure of distance.
prompt: What is the single step you could take today?

text: Sincere words are not fine; fine words are not sincere.
context: The opening line of the last chapter. Polish can be a sign that something is being sold rather than said.
prompt: Whose plain words have you overlooked because they weren't polished?

text: It is better to leave a vessel unfilled, than to attempt to carry it when it is full. If you keep feeling a point that has been sharpened, the point cannot long preserve its sharpness.
context: Laozi notes that overfilling and oversharpening both defeat their purpose: the full cup spills, the fine edge dulls. Knowing when to stop is a skill.
prompt: What are you filling to the brim that would be better left with room?

text: The partial becomes complete; the crooked, straight; the empty, full; the worn out, new. He whose desires are few gets them; he whose desires are many goes astray.
context: What bends ends up whole, what is empty gets filled, what is worn out is renewed. Those who want little get what they want; those who want much get lost.
prompt: What in your life is 'crooked' now and might yet become straight?

text: Who can make the muddy water clear? Let it be still, and it will gradually become clear.
context: Stirring muddy water only clouds it more. Left alone, the sediment settles by itself.
prompt: What might become clear if you simply stopped stirring it?

text: To know and yet think we do not know is the highest attainment; not to know and yet think we do know is a disease.
context: Laozi places wisdom in knowing the limits of our knowledge. The sick mind is not the one that doubts, but the one that is sure it already knows.
prompt: What do you think you know that you might not?

text: There is no guilt greater than to sanction ambition; no calamity greater than to be discontented with one's lot; no fault greater than the wish to be getting. Therefore the sufficiency of contentment is an enduring and unchanging sufficiency.
context: There is no greater wrong than encouraging greed, and no greater misfortune than never being satisfied. Knowing that you have enough is the only lasting wealth.
prompt: What would be enough for you, really?

text: He who devotes himself to learning seeks from day to day to increase his knowledge; he who devotes himself to the Tao seeks from day to day to diminish his doing.
context: Learning adds something every day; the Tao, Laozi's 'Way' of nature, asks us to let go of something every day. Some growth comes from doing less, not more.
prompt: What could you take away from your days rather than add?

text: All in the world know the beauty of the beautiful, and in doing this they have the idea of what ugliness is; they all know the skill of the skilful, and in doing this they have the idea of what the want of skill is.
context: As soon as we call something beautiful, we create the idea of ugly; as soon as we call someone skilful, we create the idea of clumsy. Every label creates its opposite.
prompt: Which label you use creates the very thing you dislike?

text: The softest thing in the world dashes against and overcomes the hardest; that which has no substantial existence enters where there is no crevice.
context: Water is soft, yet it wears down stone and slips through the smallest crack. Laozi sees the same quiet power in gentleness and patience.
prompt: Where could you go further by being gentler?

text: He who knows the Tao does not care to speak about it; he who is ever ready to speak about it does not know it.
context: Often quoted as 'those who know do not speak; those who speak do not know'. Deep understanding tends to be quiet.
prompt: What do you understand best, and how little do you need to say about it?

text: But I have three precious things which I prize and hold fast. The first is gentleness; the second is economy; and the third is shrinking from taking precedence of others.
context: Laozi's three treasures: gentleness, frugality, and not needing to be first.
prompt: Which of the three treasures could you practise today?

text: Man at his birth is supple and weak; at his death, firm and strong. So it is with all things. Trees and plants, in their early growth, are soft and brittle; at their death, dry and withered. Thus it is that firmness and strength are the concomitants of death; softness and weakness, the concomitants of life.
context: Living things bend; dead things are rigid. Flexibility is a sign of life, in bodies and in minds.
prompt: Where have you grown rigid, and how could you soften?

text: The farther that one goes out from himself, the less he knows.
context: Laozi's paradox for a restless age: the more we chase understanding out in the world, the less we may know ourselves. Some answers are found by staying still.
prompt: What could you understand by staying where you are?

text: The more that he expends for others, the more does he possess of his own.
context: Laozi says generosity does not empty us. What we give to others somehow enlarges what we have, in friendship, trust, and peace of mind.
prompt: What could you give today that would leave you richer?

text: People in their conduct of affairs are constantly ruining them when they are on the eve of success.
context: Many projects fail at the very end, through carelessness when success is near. Laozi asks for the same care at the end as at the beginning.
prompt: What nearly finished thing deserves your full care now?

text: You cannot speak of ocean to a well-frog,—the creature of a narrower sphere. You cannot speak of ice to a summer insect,—the creature of a season.
context: The Spirit of the Ocean speaks to a river god who thought himself great. A frog at the bottom of a well takes its circle of sky for the whole sky.
prompt: Which well are you looking up from, and how big is the sky beyond it?

text: Once upon a time, I, Chuang Tzŭ, dreamt I was a butterfly, fluttering hither and thither, to all intents and purposes a butterfly. I was conscious only of following my fancies as a butterfly, and was unconscious of my individuality as a man. Suddenly, I awaked, and there I lay, myself again. Now I do not know whether I was then a man dreaming I was a butterfly, or whether I am now a butterfly dreaming I am a man.
context: The most famous passage in Taoist literature. Zhuangzi wonders how firm the line really is between who we think we are and what we experience.
prompt: What are you sure about that might be less solid than it seems?

text: "See how the minnows are darting about! That is the pleasure of fishes." "You not being a fish yourself," said Hui Tzŭ, "how can you possibly know in what consists the pleasure of fishes?" "And you not being I," retorted Chuang Tzŭ, "how can you know that I do not know?"
context: Zhuangzi and his friend, the logician Hui Shi, argue on a bridge about whether anyone can know a fish's joy. Zhuangzi turns the logic back on him: strict proof is not the only way we know things.
prompt: Where could you simply enjoy something instead of proving it?

text: When I first began to cut up bullocks, I saw before me simply whole bullocks. After three years' practice, I saw no more whole animals. … And now I work with my mind and not with my eye.
context: Prince Hui's cook has used the same knife for nineteen years because he follows the natural gaps instead of forcing his way. Mastery means working with the grain.
prompt: Where are you hacking at something that has a natural opening?

text: "A man," replied Confucius, "does not seek to see himself in running water, but in still water. For only what is itself still can instil stillness into others."
context: Zhuangzi puts these words in the mouth of Confucius. We can only see ourselves clearly in water that is still.
prompt: How could you become still enough to see yourself clearly?

text: It is wood of no quality, and of no use. That is why it has attained its present age.
context: A carpenter dismisses a huge old tree as worthless. That evening the tree appears in his dream: being 'useless' is what let it grow so old.
prompt: What 'useless' thing in your life is actually keeping you whole?

text: Great knowledge embraces the whole: small knowledge, a part only.
context: Zhuangzi contrasts two kinds of knowing: small knowledge grabs one part and takes it for everything; great knowledge keeps the whole picture in view.
prompt: What part of a situation have you been mistaking for the whole?

text: My life has a limit, but my knowledge is without limit. To drive the limited in search of the limitless, is fatal; and the knowledge of those who do this is fatally lost.
context: Zhuangzi warns against trying to know everything. A limited life spent chasing limitless knowledge is exhausted before it gets anywhere.
prompt: What are you trying to master that could never be finished?

text: When she died, I could not help being affected by her death. … passing from one phase to another like the sequence of spring, summer, autumn, and winter.
context: When Zhuangzi's wife dies, his friend finds him singing and drumming on a bowl. He grieved, he explains, and then saw her death as part of nature's turning seasons.
prompt: Which ending in your life could you see as a change of season?

text: For the perfect man employs his mind as a mirror. It grasps nothing: it refuses nothing. It receives, but does not keep.
context: Zhuangzi uses the mirror as a picture of a free mind: it reflects whatever comes, clearly and fully, and holds on to nothing once it has gone.
prompt: What are you still holding that you could simply let pass through?

text: Life is a loan with which the borrower does but add more dust and dirt to the sum total of existence. Life and death are as day and night.
context: Life is only borrowed, and life and death follow each other like day and night. A man says this calmly after a strange growth appears on his elbow.
prompt: If your life is a loan, what are you doing with it?

text: The mushroom of a morning knows not the alternation of day and night. The chrysalis knows not the alternation of spring and autumn.
context: Every creature measures the world by its own lifespan. Zhuangzi invites us to imagine much longer and shorter scales than our own.
prompt: How would today's worry look on the scale of a hundred years?

text: The Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao. The name that can be named is not the enduring and unchanging name.
context: The famous opening of the Tao Te Ching. The deepest reality, Laozi warns, can't be fully captured in words, including his own.
prompt: What matters to you that words never quite capture?

text: In the highest antiquity, the people did not know that there were their rulers. In the next age they loved them and praised them. In the next they feared them; in the next they despised them. … Their work was done and their undertakings were successful, while the people all said, 'We are as we are, of ourselves!'
context: Laozi ranks leaders: the best are barely noticed, and when the work is done, people feel they did it themselves.
prompt: Would the people you lead say they did it themselves?

text: He who stands on his tiptoes does not stand firm; he who stretches his legs does not walk easily. So, he who displays himself does not shine; he who asserts his own views is not distinguished; …
context: Straining to look bigger makes us unsteady. Showing off rarely earns the respect it seeks.
prompt: Where are you standing on tiptoe?

text: Or fame or life, / Which do you hold more dear? / Or life or wealth, / To which would you adhere? … Who is content / Needs fear no shame. / Who knows to stop / Incurs no blame.
context: A simple test of priorities: if you had to choose between fame or wealth and your own life, which would you keep? Knowing when to stop keeps us safe.
prompt: What are you trading your life for?

text: All difficult things in the world are sure to arise from a previous state in which they were easy, and all great things from one in which they were small.
context: Deal with problems while they are small, and build great things step by step.
prompt: Which small problem today could become a big one if you ignore it?

text: That whereby the rivers and seas are able to receive the homage and tribute of all the valley streams, is their skill in being lower than they; … So it is that the sage ruler, wishing to be above men, puts himself by his words below them, and, wishing to be before them, places his person behind them.
context: The sea gathers all rivers because it lies lowest. Laozi's model of leadership is humble service, long before the modern phrase 'servant leadership'.
prompt: How could you lead by putting yourself lower?

text: Therefore the sage puts his own person last, and yet it is found in the foremost place; …
context: Those who don't push themselves forward often end up trusted and in front.
prompt: When did putting others first bring you forward?

text: He who would so win it destroys it; he who would hold it in his grasp loses it.
context: Laozi is speaking about power over a kingdom, but the lesson fits much else: grip something too hard and it slips away.
prompt: What are you gripping so hard that it's slipping away?

text: Governing a great state is like cooking small fish.
context: Small fish fall apart if you keep stirring them. Good leaders don't keep interfering.
prompt: Where would less interference from you help things work?

text: Who thinks his great achievements poor / Shall find his vigour long endure.
context: Those who don't rest on their successes keep their energy longer.
prompt: Which success are you resting on too comfortably?

text: Favour and disgrace would seem equally to be feared; …
context: Praise and blame both make us dependent on others' opinion. Laozi advises being free from both.
prompt: Does praise unsettle you as much as criticism?

text: He who in Tao's wars has skill / Assumes no martial port; / He who fights with most good will / To rage makes no resort.
context: Laozi describes the skilled fighter in a short verse: the strongest don't look aggressive, and the best don't need anger. Real strength is calm.
prompt: Where could you be firm without being angry?

text: May not the Way of Heaven be compared to the method of bending a bow? The part of the bow which was high is brought low, and what was low is raised up.
context: Nature balances itself, lowering what is too high and lifting what is too low. Laozi wishes human society did the same.
prompt: Where is your life out of balance, and what needs lowering or raising?

text: A duck's legs, for instance, are short, but if we try to lengthen them, it occasions pain; and a crane's legs are long, but if we try to cut off a portion of them, it produces grief.
context: Each creature is right as it is. Forcing anyone to fit a single standard causes suffering.
prompt: Where are you trying to 'lengthen' or 'shorten' yourself or someone else?

text: Was it better for the tortoise to die, and leave its shell to be thus honoured? Or would it have been better for it to live, and keep on dragging its tail through the mud? … Go your ways. I will keep on drawing my tail after me through the mud.
context: Offered a high office, Zhuangzi points to a sacred tortoise shell kept in a temple. He'd rather be alive and free in the mud than honoured and dead.
prompt: What honour would cost you your freedom?

text: A keeper of monkeys, in giving them out their acorns, once said, 'In the morning I will give you three measures and in the evening four.' This made them all angry, and he said, 'Very well. In the morning I will give you four and in the evening three.'
context: The monkeys got the same amount either way, but one version made them happy. We too react to how things are framed.
prompt: Which of your reactions depends on framing more than substance?

text: If a man is crossing a river in a boat, and another empty vessel comes into collision with it, even though he be a man of a choleric temper, he will not be angry with it. … If a man can empty himself of himself, during his time in the world, who can harm him?
context: We don't get angry at an empty boat that bumps us, only at one with someone in it. Zhuangzi suggests being like the empty boat: without an ego to bruise.
prompt: What would bump into you without hurting if you took it less personally?

text: Fishing-stakes are employed to catch fish; but when the fish are got, the men forget the stakes. … Words are employed to convey ideas; but when the ideas are apprehended, men forget the words.
context: Words are tools for catching ideas. Once we understand, we no longer need to hold onto the exact words.
prompt: What idea do you understand well enough to forget the words you learned it in?

text: He who is contending for a piece of earthenware puts forth all his skill.
context: Zhuangzi goes on: shooting for a brass buckle, the archer grows nervous; shooting for gold, he is as if blind. The more the prize matters, the more it spoils our skill.
prompt: Where does caring too much about the prize make you clumsy?

text: To look at him, you would say he was a cock of wood.
context: A trainer prepares a fighting cock for forty days, until it no longer reacts to other birds. Its calm makes rivals flee. Mastery looks like stillness.
prompt: What would it look like for you to be calm as wood under provocation?

text: Perfect enjoyment is to be without enjoyment; the highest praise is to be without praise.
context: Zhuangzi turns our ideas upside down: the deepest happiness doesn't chase pleasures, and the greatest worth doesn't need praise. Wanting them is what keeps us restless.
prompt: What do you enjoy without needing anything from it?

text: The marquis was trying to nourish the bird with what he used for himself …
context: A ruler welcomes a sea-bird with feasts and royal music, and it dies of fear in three days. Caring for others means giving them what they need, not what we like.
prompt: Who are you caring for in your way rather than theirs?

text: In making a wheel, if I proceed gently, that is pleasant enough, but the workmanship is not strong; if I proceed violently, that is toilsome and the joinings do not fit. If the movements of my hand are neither too gentle nor too violent, the idea in my mind is realised. But I cannot tell how to do this by word of mouth; there is a knack in it.
context: Wheelwright Phien tells a duke that the books he reads are only the leftovers of dead sages. Real skill lives in the hands and can't be put into words.
prompt: What do you know how to do that you could never fully explain?

text: Horses can with their hoofs tread on the hoarfrost and snow, and with their hair withstand the wind and cold; they feed on the grass and drink water; they prance with their legs and leap:—this is the true nature of horses.
context: Zhuangzi goes on to describe how a famous trainer broke horses with brands and bridles, and many died. Forcing living things against their nature harms them.
prompt: What part of your true nature has been trained out of you?

text: All things alike go through their processes of activity, and then we see them return to their original state. When things in the vegetable world have displayed their luxuriant growth, we see each of them return to its root. This returning to their root is what we call the state of stillness.
context: Laozi watches plants grow, flourish, and return to their roots. Rest and return are part of life's cycle, not its failure; stillness is where growth begins again.
prompt: What root do you need to return to?

text: The skilful traveller leaves no traces of his wheels or footsteps; the skilful speaker says nothing that can be found fault with or blamed.
context: Laozi says real skill leaves no visible trace of effort. The best traveller, speaker, or leader works so naturally that no one notices how hard it was.
prompt: What do you do so naturally that nobody sees the effort?

text: Is it not pleasant to learn with a constant perseverance and application? Is it not delightful to have friends coming from distant quarters? Is he not a man of complete virtue, who feels no discomposure though men may take no note of him?
context: The opening lines of the Analects, the sayings of Confucius collected by his students. Learning, friendship and not needing recognition: the whole book in three questions.
prompt: Which of the three would make today a good day: learning something, seeing a friend, or not needing to be noticed?

text: I will not be afflicted at men's not knowing me; I will be afflicted that I do not know men.
context: Confucius turns a common worry around. Instead of fretting that others don't understand us, he asks whether we understand them.
prompt: Who in your life might you not yet really know?

text: If a man keeps cherishing his old knowledge, so as continually to be acquiring new, he may be a teacher of others.
context: Good teachers keep returning to what they know until it yields something new. Old knowledge is not a shelf but a garden.
prompt: What do you already know that might teach you something new if you went back to it?

text: Learning without thought is labour lost; thought without learning is perilous.
context: Reading without reflecting changes nothing; reflecting without learning goes round in circles. Confucius wants both, together.
prompt: Are you lately more at risk of learning without thinking, or thinking without learning?

text: When you know a thing, to hold that you know it; and when you do not know a thing, to allow that you do not know it;— this is knowledge.
context: Spoken to Zilu, a bold student who was quick to speak. Like Socrates, Confucius places wisdom in being honest about where our knowledge ends.
prompt: Where do you pretend to know more than you do?

text: He acts before he speaks, and afterwards speaks according to his actions.
context: Asked what makes a person of true quality, Confucius points to the order of things: first do it, then talk about it.
prompt: What are you talking about doing that you could simply start?

text: I am not concerned that I have no place, I am concerned how I may fit myself for one. I am not concerned that I am not known, I seek to be worthy to be known.
context: Confucius spent years without the position he hoped for. He suggests turning the worry about recognition into work on oneself.
prompt: What would make you worthy of the place you want, whether or not you get it?

text: When we see men of worth, we should think of equalling them; when we see men of a contrary character, we should turn inwards and examine ourselves.
context: Everyone we meet is a lesson: the admirable show us what to aim for, the others what to look for in ourselves.
prompt: Whose behaviour annoyed you recently, and is any of it in you too?

text: Virtue is not left to stand alone. He who practises it will have neighbors.
context: Confucius reassures those who try to live well: goodness may feel lonely at first, but it draws like-minded people to it in time.
prompt: Who has your kindness quietly drawn closer to you?

text: Admirable indeed was the virtue of Hui! With a single bamboo dish of rice, a single gourd dish of drink, and living in his mean narrow lane, while others could not have endured the distress, he did not allow his joy to be affected by it.
context: Yan Hui was Confucius' favourite student, poor all his life and dead young. His joy did not depend on what he owned.
prompt: What joy of yours would survive losing your comforts?

text: They who know the truth are not equal to those who love it, and they who love it are not equal to those who delight in it.
context: Confucius describes three stages in our relationship with anything worth learning: knowing it, loving it, and finally finding real delight in it.
prompt: What do you know well but no longer delight in?

text: The wise find pleasure in water; the virtuous find pleasure in hills. The wise are active; the virtuous are tranquil. The wise are joyful; the virtuous are long-lived.
context: Water moves and adapts; hills stay put. Confucius sees two temperaments, the quick mind and the steady heart, and honours both.
prompt: Are you more water or hill these days, and what could the other teach you?

text: With coarse rice to eat, with water to drink, and my bended arm for a pillow;— I have still joy in the midst of these things. Riches and honours acquired by unrighteousness, are to me as a floating cloud.
context: Confucius on simple living. Wealth gained wrongly means as little to him as a cloud drifting past.
prompt: What simple thing gives you joy that money couldn't improve?

text: When I walk along with two others, they may serve me as my teachers. I will select their good qualities and follow them, their bad qualities and avoid them.
context: Confucius says any two companions can teach us: the good qualities of one show us what to follow, the faults of the other what to avoid in ourselves.
prompt: What did the last two people you spent time with teach you?

text: Is virtue a thing remote? I wish to be virtuous, and lo! virtue is at hand.
context: Confucius insists goodness is not far away, waiting for the perfect moment. It begins the moment we sincerely want it.
prompt: What good thing are you postponing that you could begin right now?

text: Learn as if you could not reach your object, and were always fearing also lest you should lose it.
context: Confucius describes the eager student: always reaching ahead, and holding on to what was learned as if it might slip away.
prompt: What are you learning that deserves this kind of eagerness?

text: There were four things from which the Master was entirely free. He had no foregone conclusions, no arbitrary predeterminations, no obstinacy, and no egoism.
context: Confucius had four qualities his students admired: he didn't jump to conclusions, wasn't rigid, wasn't stubborn, and wasn't self-centred.
prompt: Which of the four do you hold on to most tightly?

text: It passes on just like this, not ceasing day or night!
context: Confucius, standing by a river, watches it flow without pause. He sees life passing the same way, which makes every moment worth using well.
prompt: What is flowing past you right now that you would like to notice?

text: The commander of the forces of a large state may be carried off, but the will of even a common man cannot be taken from him.
context: Confucius says an army can lose its general, but no one can take away a person's will. Even the most ordinary life holds this inner freedom.
prompt: What choice is entirely yours today, whatever happens around you?

text: When the year becomes cold, then we know how the pine and the cypress are the last to lose their leaves.
context: Pines and cypresses stay green through winter. Character, like an evergreen, shows itself in the hard seasons.
prompt: Who stayed green for you during a hard winter?

text: To go beyond is as wrong as to fall short.
context: Asked which of two students was better, one who overdid things and one who fell short, Confucius refused to choose. The ideal is the balanced middle, the due mean, much like Aristotle's.
prompt: Where are you overdoing something, and where falling short?

text: When internal examination discovers nothing wrong, what is there to be anxious about, what is there to fear?
context: Asked about the person of true quality, Confucius says they live without anxiety or fear, not because life is safe but because their conscience is clear.
prompt: What would clear your conscience enough to let a worry go?

text: To be poor without murmuring is difficult. To be rich without being proud is easy.
context: Confucius is honest about which test is harder. Grace in hardship asks far more of us than modesty in comfort.
prompt: What difficulty could you carry today without complaining about it?

text: In ancient times, men learned with a view to their own improvement. Now-a-days, men learn with a view to the approbation of others.
context: A complaint from 2,500 years ago that sounds very modern: learning to grow, versus learning to impress.
prompt: Is there something you study mainly so that others will notice?

text: With what then will you recompense kindness? Recompense injury with justice, and recompense kindness with kindness.
context: Someone asks whether we should repay injury with kindness. Confucius replies with a question: then what is left for those who are kind to us? Fairness for harm, kindness for kindness.
prompt: Where would fairness serve better than forced kindness, or the other way round?

text: He who requires much from himself and little from others, will keep himself from being the object of resentment.
context: Confucius offers a simple recipe for fewer grudges: high standards for ourselves, generous ones for others. It protects our relationships in both directions.
prompt: Whom are you holding to a higher standard than you hold yourself?

text: What the superior man seeks, is in himself. What the mean man seeks, is in others.
context: 'Superior man' is the old translation of junzi, a person of noble character. Such a person looks inward for causes and remedies; the petty person looks for someone to blame.
prompt: What are you seeking from others that you could find in yourself?

text: What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.
context: Asked for one word to live by, Confucius chose shu, reciprocity, and summed it up in this line: a version of the golden rule found in many cultures.
prompt: Where today could you treat someone the way you would want to be treated?

text: By nature, men are nearly alike; by practice, they get to be wide apart.
context: We start out much the same; what we do again and again makes us different. Aristotle would have agreed.
prompt: Which daily habit is quietly shaping who you are becoming?

text: The faults of the superior man are like the eclipses of the sun and moon. He has his faults, and all men see them; he changes again, and all men look up to him.
context: Zigong, a student of Confucius, on how a good person handles mistakes: openly, in full view, and then changed.
prompt: Which mistake of yours could you own more openly?

text: To have faults and not to reform them,— this, indeed, should be pronounced having faults.
context: Confucius accepts mistakes as human. The real fault, he says, is refusing to correct them once we know.
prompt: Which of your faults have you made peace with that you could still change?

text: The man of perfect virtue is cautious and slow in his speech.
context: Confucius distrusted quick talkers. Speaking slowly leaves time to check that our words match what we will actually do.
prompt: When did speaking too quickly cost you?

text: The superior man seeks to perfect the admirable qualities of men, and does not seek to perfect their bad qualities.
context: 'Superior man' is Legge's word for junzi, a person of noble character. Such a person helps others grow in what is good in them, not in their worst habits.
prompt: Whose good qualities could you help grow?

text: To govern means to rectify. If you lead on the people with correctness, who will dare not to be correct?
context: A ruler asks Confucius about government. His answer: lead by your own example, and others will follow.
prompt: What would change around you if you set a better example?

text: Let your evinced desires be for what is good, and the people will be good.
context: When a ruler suggests killing wrongdoers, Confucius replies that people follow what their leader visibly wants. He goes on: the leader is like the wind, the people like grass that bends with it.
prompt: What do the people around you see you wanting?

text: Faithfully admonish your friend, and skillfully lead him on. If you find him impracticable, stop.
context: Good friends tell each other hard truths, gently. But Confucius adds a limit: if they won't listen, stop, before you lose the friendship.
prompt: Is there a friend you need to speak to honestly, or stop pushing?

text: The superior man on grounds of culture meets with his friends, and by their friendship helps his virtue.
context: Shared learning and interests bring friends together, and good friends help each other become better.
prompt: Which friend makes you a better person?

text: When a prince's personal conduct is correct, his government is effective without the issuing of orders.
context: A leader whose own behaviour is right hardly needs to give orders. People follow example more than instructions.
prompt: Where are you giving orders instead of setting an example?

text: The superior man is easy to serve and difficult to please.
context: A person of quality is easy to work for, because they don't ask for flattery, but hard to please, because they expect what is right.
prompt: Are you easy to work with, or easy to please?

text: The superior man has a dignified ease without pride. The mean man has pride without a dignified ease.
context: Real confidence is relaxed; pride is tense. Confucius contrasts the person of quality with the 'mean' or petty person.
prompt: Where are you proud without being at ease?

text: When the love of superiority, boasting, resentments, and covetousness are repressed, this may be deemed perfect virtue.
context: A student lists four faults he has overcome and asks if that is perfect virtue. Confucius replies that it is difficult, but he is not sure it is enough: goodness is more than avoiding faults.
prompt: Which of the four, superiority, boasting, resentment, or envy, do you still struggle with?

text: There is no greater delight than to be conscious of sincerity on self-examination.
context: Mencius (c. 372–289 BCE) was Confucius' greatest follower. For him, the deepest joy comes from looking inside and finding nothing false.
prompt: When you look honestly at yourself, what do you find?

text: The sense of shame is to a man of great importance.
context: Mencius saw shame not as a burden but as a moral compass. Someone who feels no shame has lost something essential.
prompt: What does your sense of shame protect you from?

text: Let a man not do what his own sense of righteousness tells him not to do …
context: Mencius believed we already know right from wrong. The work is to listen to that inner sense.
prompt: What is your conscience telling you not to do?

text: …if men suddenly see a child about to fall into a well, they will without exception experience a feeling of alarm and distress.
context: Mencius' famous argument that humans are naturally good: anyone seeing a child about to fall feels an immediate urge to help, before any thought of reward.
prompt: When did you feel an instant urge to help someone?

text: The feeling of commiseration is the principle of benevolence.
context: Mencius, Confucius' great follower, saw compassion as a seed of goodness in every person. Looked after, it grows into kindness toward everyone.
prompt: How do you tend the seed of compassion in yourself?

text: I daily examine myself on three points:— whether, in transacting business for others, I may have been not faithful;— whether, in intercourse with friends, I may have been not sincere;— whether I may have not mastered and practised the instructions of my teacher.
context: Zengzi, one of Confucius' students, describes his daily review: Was I reliable for others? Was I sincere with friends? Did I practise what I was taught?
prompt: Run through Zengzi's three questions for today. Which one makes you pause?

text: The prosecution of learning may be compared to what may happen in raising a mound. If there want but one basket of earth to complete the work, and I stop, the stopping is my own work. It may be compared to throwing down the earth on the level ground. Though but one basketful is thrown at a time, the advancing with it is my own going forward.
context: Confucius compares learning to building a mound one basket of earth at a time. Whether we stop one basket short or keep going, the choice is always ours.
prompt: What are you one basket away from finishing, or from starting?

text: The perfect circle of the full moon lasts only for a very short time; soon it begins to wane, though one who pays no attention to it may think that in a single night there is little or no change perceptible.
context: Kenkō was a 14th-century poet and monk whose short essays on beauty and impermanence remain beloved in Japan. Change, he notes, is often too slow to see.
prompt: What is quietly changing in your life, too slowly to notice?

text: A certain man who was learning archery faced the target with two arrows in his hand. But his instructor said, ‘A beginner ought never to have a second arrow; for as long as he relies upon the other, he will be careless with his first one. At each shot he ought to think that he is bound to settle it with this particular shaft at any cost.’
context: A teacher tells his student to carry only one arrow, because a second one makes the first careless. Kenkō applies it to every moment of life.
prompt: What 'second arrow' is making you careless with the first?

text: Is it only when the flowers are in full bloom and when the moon is shining in spotless perfection that we ought to gaze at them? … The twigs which bear no blossoms as yet and a garden strewn with withered petals are equally to be admired.
context: Kenkō's most famous essay. Beauty isn't only in the peak moment, but in anticipation, in absence, and in what has already passed.
prompt: What 'not yet' or 'no longer' could you admire today?

text: The dew upon Adashi Moor never fades away, nor is Toribe Moor ever free from smoke; what a state of things we should have, were our existence never to be cut short! There would be no feelings of pity left in the world. Far better is it to have no certainty as to the length of life.
context: If we lived forever, we would lose all tenderness; it is better not to know how long we have. Adashi Moor and Toribe Moor were burial grounds near Kyoto, so their dew and smoke stand for death.
prompt: How does knowing life is uncertain make it more precious to you?

text: Nothing is more refreshing than to make friends with those who are no longer to be seen in this life by means of an open book, a lamp, and solitude.
context: Kenkō, a 14th-century Japanese monk, describes the pleasure of reading alone at night by lamplight. A book lets us befriend people who died long ago.
prompt: Which writer from the past would you like to spend an evening with?

text: The order of the four seasons is fixed, while none know the time of death; it comes not from in front, but ever presses on from behind.
context: Seasons arrive in order; death doesn't announce itself. Kenkō's image: the tide comes in while the beach still looks dry.
