prompt: What would you stop postponing if you felt time pressing from behind?

text: He who afflicts his whole life by spending it in the pursuit of riches and fame, leaving himself no leisure for quiet, is but a fool.
context: Kenkō judges a life spent chasing wealth and reputation, with no time left for quiet, as foolish. Riches, he adds, cannot even protect their owner.
prompt: Is there enough leisure for quiet in your life?

text: How can a man ever find it wearisome to live at leisure? Free from surrounding cares, it is good merely to be alone.
context: Kenkō defends solitude: away from the noise of the world, we stop being blown about by everyone else's moods.
prompt: When did you last enjoy being alone?

text: He who mixes with the experts while he is himself still stiff and imperfect, and is not ashamed when others laugh and mock at him, will enjoy overcoming such discouragement; and, though he have not the natural talent for it, he will not lag far behind the others.
context: Someone who practises among experts while still clumsy, and doesn't mind being laughed at, will in time catch up even without natural talent. Kenkō's case for being an open beginner.
prompt: What are you avoiding because you're not good at it yet?

text: You may propose to do a certain thing to-day, but some unforeseen matter of importance crops up and you spend the time wrongly on it; or perhaps somebody you had expected cannot come, and some unexpected visitor arrives instead. At all events you fail to do what you had planned, and it is only the unlooked for that actually happens.
context: Kenkō on plans: the day rarely goes as expected, and neither do years. Better to hold plans lightly.
prompt: What unexpected thing happened today, and what did it bring?

text: Generally speaking, uniformity in anything at all is bad; it is better to leave a little imperfection.
context: Kenkō praises frayed silk covers and mismatched books. Perfection, he suggests, leaves nothing to grow into.
prompt: Where could a little imperfection make something better?

text: The moon when full begins to wane; where there has been increase there is bound to be decrease; and in every case he who has reached the very front soon gets a set-back.
context: Kenkō observes that every full moon starts to wane, and every peak begins a descent. He uses it to warn against chasing the very top.
prompt: Where could you be content with less than the very top?

text: Nothing is harder to forsake than the customs and conventionalities of life, whatever they may be.
context: Kenkō notices how hard it is to step away from social customs and obligations, even when we know they keep us from what matters most.
prompt: Which convention are you keeping only out of habit?

text: Those who cannot feel the littleness of great things in themselves are apt to overlook the greatness of little things in others.
source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. I
context: People who can't see their own smallness miss the greatness of small things in others. Okakura aimed this at Westerners who mocked the tea ceremony as quaint.
prompt: What small thing in someone else have you overlooked?

text: Let us dream of evanescence, and linger in the beautiful foolishness of things.
source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. I
context: Okakura invites us to accept that everything passes, and to enjoy the lovely, silly little things while they last. 'Evanescence' means passing quickly.
prompt: What passing thing could you linger over today?

text: The art of life lies in a constant readjustment to our surroundings.
source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. III
context: Kakuzo Okakura wrote The Book of Tea in English in 1906 to explain Japanese culture to the West. Drawing on Taoism, he says living well means constantly adjusting, not following a fixed recipe.
prompt: What change around you are you resisting instead of adjusting to?

text: Perhaps we reveal ourselves too much in small things because we have so little of the great to conceal.
source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. II
context: Maybe we give ourselves away in small things because we have little that is grand to hide. A wry, self-mocking line by Okakura.
prompt: What do your small daily habits say about you?

text: The usefulness of a water pitcher dwelt in the emptiness where water might be put, not in the form of the pitcher or the material of which it was made. … One who could make of himself a vacuum into which others might freely enter would become master of all situations.
source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. III
context: A pitcher is useful because of its empty space, not its shape or material. A person who leaves room for others can handle any situation. Okakura borrows the idea from Laozi.
prompt: How could you leave more room for others to enter?

text: True beauty could be discovered only by one who mentally completed the incomplete. The virility of life and art lay in its possibilities for growth.
source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. IV
context: Real beauty is found by those who complete in their minds what is left unfinished. Life and art stay alive by leaving room to grow. In the tea room, things are left incomplete on purpose.
prompt: What unfinished thing could you appreciate as it is?

text: In leaving something unsaid the beholder is given a chance to complete the idea and thus a great masterpiece irresistibly rivets your attention until you seem to become actually a part of it.
source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. III
context: Okakura says great art does not spell everything out. It leaves space for us to complete it, and in that space we become part of the work.
prompt: What could you leave unsaid today, and let someone else complete?

text: He only who has lived with the beautiful can die beautifully.
source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. VII
context: Okakura writes of the great tea masters, who met even their deaths with the grace they had practised all their lives.
prompt: What beauty are you living with every day?

text: "Young fool," chided the tea-master, "that is not the way a garden path should be swept." Saying this, Rikiu stepped into the garden, shook a tree and scattered over the garden gold and crimson leaves, scraps of the brocade of autumn!
source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. IV
context: The tea master Rikyū's lesson to a son who had swept the garden perfectly clean: real beauty needs a touch of the natural.
prompt: Where could you allow a few leaves to fall?

text: One cannot listen to different pieces of music at the same time, a real comprehension of the beautiful being possible only through concentration upon some central motive.
source: Kakuzo Okakura, The Book of Tea, ch. IV
context: In the Japanese tea room, only one beautiful object is shown at a time. Okakura sees in this a lesson about attention in general: we appreciate deeply only what we focus on.
prompt: What one thing deserves your full attention today?

text: The current of a running stream flows on unceasingly, but the water is not the same: the foam floating on the pool where it lingers, now vanishes and now forms again, but is never lasting. Such are mankind and their habitations.
context: The famous opening of Hōjōki ('An Account of My Ten-Foot Hut', 1212), written by a poet who withdrew to a tiny mountain hut after years of fire, famine and earthquake.
prompt: What in your life is the same river, but different water?

text: It is barely ten feet square, and only seven feet high. As it was not meant for a fixed abode, the ground about it was trodden hard and left uncultivated. The walls are of mud, and it is thatched with rushes. The joints are fastened with rings and staples, for the greater convenience of removal elsewhere if any subject of dissatisfaction should arise. How little trouble it would take to rebuild it in another place!
context: Chōmei's last home was a hut small enough to take apart and move on two carts. Owning little, he could not lose much.
prompt: What could you live without, and how would that lighten you?

text: When I first took up my abode in this place, I thought it was only for a little while. But five years have passed and my temporary hut has become old. Under the eaves there is a deep bed of withered leaves, and moss has gathered on the earthen floor.
context: Chōmei meant his hut to be temporary. Five years later, moss covers the floor. Life settles in while we're still telling ourselves it's for a little while.
prompt: What 'temporary' arrangement in your life has quietly become permanent?

text: When on a calm night the moon shines in at my window, I think with yearning of the men of old.
context: Alone in his hut, Chōmei finds company in the moon and in the memory of those who lived before him.
prompt: Who from the past do you feel close to on a quiet night?

text: Things which Excite Regrets for the Past: Withered hollyhocks. On a wet day to turn over the letters of a person once loved by us. Last year's fans. Bright moonlight nights.

text:

text:

text:

prompt: Where are you settling for the reflection instead of the real thing?

text:

text:

text: …the body may be figured as a kingdom, the soul as its king … Reason may be called the vizier, or prime minister, passion the revenue-collector, and anger the police-officer.

text:

text:

text:

text:

source: Rumi, Masnavi, Book III, 'The Vakil of the Prince of Bokhara'
context: What grows in a life, words, actions, and habits, starts in the heart. Tend the root and the branches follow.

text:
Pass over names and look to qualities,
So that qualities may lead you to essence!
source: Rumi, Masnavi, Book II, 'The Tree of Life'

prompt: Are you chasing a title or label rather than the quality behind it?

text:

text:

text:

text:

text:

Roll up its waste of waters, from the land

To mark what evils we ourselves be spared;
It is sweet, again, to view the mighty strife
Of armies embattled yonder o'er the plains,
Ourselves no sharers in the peril; but nothing
There is more goodly than to hold the high

text: Accustom yourself to believe that death is nothing to us, for good and evil imply sentience, and death is the privation of all sentience; therefore a right understanding that death is nothing to us makes the mortality of life enjoyable, not by adding to life an illimitable time, but by taking away the yearning after immortality.

text: It is therefore not of small moment whether we are trained from childhood in one set of habits or another; on the contrary it is of very great, or rather of supreme, importance.

text: The perfect form of friendship is that between the good, and those who resemble each other in virtue. prompt: Which of your friendships rest on usefulness, pleasure, or goodness?

text: We regard independence of outward things as a great good, not so as in all cases to use little, but so as to be contented with little if we have not much, being honestly persuaded that they have the sweetest enjoyment of luxury who stand least in need of it, and that whatever is natural is easily procured and only the vain and worthless hard to win.

prompt: What could you happily do without?

text: To be beneficent when we can is a duty; and besides this, there are many minds so sympathetically constituted that, without any other motive of vanity or self-interest, they find a pleasure in spreading joy around them and can take delight in the satisfaction of others so far as it is their own work.

prompt: Where is kindness easy for you, and where would it take principle?

text: Nobody ever grudges a moment of time; but is that altogether wise of him, or foolish? text: Capacity for the nobler feelings is in most natures a very tender plant, easily killed, not only by hostile influences, but by mere want of sustenance.

text: A good will appears to constitute the indispensable condition even of being worthy of happiness.

prompt: What would make you feel you had earned your happiness?

text: There is nothing in the world more soft and weak than water, and yet for attacking things that are firm and strong there is nothing that can take precedence of it;—for there is nothing so effectual for which it can be changed. context: Water wears down stone. Everyone knows that softness can win, says Laozi, yet hardly anyone lives by it.

text: A man is temperate if he abstains from bodily pleasures and finds this abstinence itself enjoyable, profligate if he feels it irksome.

prompt: Which good habit has started to feel natural, and which still feels forced?

text: Duty! prompt: Which duty do you respect, even when you don't feel like doing it?

text: My misfortune is that I am interested in too many things, and not decisively committed to any one thing, to which I might subordinate everything else.

text: The beginning is admittedly more than half of the whole.
context: Getting the starting point right shapes everything that follows.
prompt: What are you starting now, and is the starting point right?

text: Wherefore prudence is a more precious thing even than philosophy; from it spring all the other virtues, for it teaches that we cannot lead a life of pleasure which is not also a life of prudence, honour, and justice; nor lead a life of prudence, honour, and justice, which is not also a life of pleasure. context: For Epicurus, a pleasant life and a good life are the same thing: you cannot have one without the other.

text: He judges, therefore, that he can do a certain thing because he is conscious that he ought, and he recognizes that he is free…

text: The main constituents of a satisfied life appear to be two, either of which by itself is often found sufficient for the purpose: tranquillity, and excitement. context: Calm and stimulation: Mill thought most people need some balance of both to be content.
prompt: Does your life need more tranquillity, or more excitement, right now?

text: Every man loves himself more than all the rest of men, but yet sets less value on his own opinion of himself than on the opinion of others.
context: A puzzled observation from the last book of the Meditations: we care most about ourselves, yet trust others' view of us more than our own.
prompt: Whose opinion of you counts for more than your own, and why?

text: These sons belong to me, and this wealth belongs to me," with such thoughts a fool is tormented. He himself does not belong to himself; how much less sons and wealth?"
context: A reflection on possession: we say 'mine' about people and things, yet we do not even fully own ourselves.
prompt: What do you call 'mine' that you might hold more loosely?

text: Death is nothing to us; for the body, when it has been resolved into its elements, has no feeling, and that which has no feeling is nothing to us.
context: The second of Epicurus' forty core teachings, memorised by his followers. Death cannot harm one who no longer feels.
prompt: What fear might shrink if you looked at it this plainly?

text: Fontenelle says, "I bow before a great man, but my mind does not bow." context: Rank and talent may impress us, but only good character commands real inner respect.
prompt: Whose quiet goodness do you respect most?

text: Every man lives only this present time, which is an indivisible point, and that all the rest of his life is either past or it is uncertain.
context: The past is gone and the future unknown; the only life anyone actually lives is the present moment.
prompt: What would change if you gave this moment your whole attention?

text: It is not easy to define in what manner and with whom and on what grounds and how long one ought to be angry, and up to what point one does right in so doing and where error begins.

prompt: When was your anger last right, and when was it not?

text: Because his example exhibits to me a law that humbles my self-conceit when I compare it with my conduct: a law, the practicability of obedience to which I see proved by fact before my eyes.
context: A good person's example humbles us because it proves that goodness is possible.
prompt: Whose example shows you what is possible?

text: Continuous pain does not last long in the flesh; on the contrary, pain, if extreme, is present a very short time, and even that degree of pain which barely outweighs pleasure in the flesh does not last for many days together.
context: Epicurus himself suffered from painful illness. His teaching was that severe pain is brief and long pain is bearable.
prompt: What pain have you endured that turned out more bearable than you feared?

text: Let us, then, take the argument as our guide, which has revealed to us that the best way of life is to practise justice and every virtue in life and death.
context: The closing words of the Gorgias. After a long and heated argument, Socrates concludes simply: practise justice and every virtue.
prompt: What would it mean to follow the argument wherever it leads?

text: From this moment my burden grew lighter. The oppression of the thought that all feeling was dead within me was gone. I was no longer hopeless: I was not a stock or a stone. context: Mill describes the moment his depression began to lift: reading a moving story, he cried, and realised he could still feel.
prompt: When did you last feel something deeply, and what did it tell you?

text: Men exist for the sake of one another. Teach them then, or bear with them.
context: The Stoics saw humans as social by nature. When others fall short, there are only two fitting responses: help them see, or be patient.
prompt: Is there someone you could teach, or someone you need to bear with?

text: Ask him, however- if his sovereign ordered him, on pain of the same immediate execution, to bear false witness against an honourable man, whom the prince might wish to destroy under a plausible pretext, would he consider it possible in that case to overcome his love of life, however great it may be.

prompt: What would you refuse to do, whatever it cost?

text: The happiness which forms the utilitarian standard of what is right in conduct, is not the agent's own happiness, but that of all concerned. As between his own happiness and that of others, utilitarianism requires him to be as strictly impartial as a disinterested and benevolent spectator.
context: Utilitarianism counts everyone's happiness equally, your own included but no more than anyone else's.
prompt: How would you decide if your own happiness counted no more than another's?

text: In a particular flower I may train myself to see the whole world; or I may listen to the many hints and suggestions which Nature offers with respect to human life.

prompt: What small thing near you could you look at long enough to learn from?

text: Persons who wish another good for his own sake, if the feeling is not reciprocated, are merely said to feel goodwill for him: only when mutual is such goodwill termed friendship. And perhaps we should also add the qualification that the feeling of goodwill must be known to its object.

prompt: Who might not know how much goodwill you feel toward them?

text: This is virtue, and virtue, at least as a naturally acquired faculty, can never be perfect.
context: Virtue, for Kant, is steady progress rather than a finished state.

text: A person whose desires and impulses are his own—are the expression of his own nature, as it has been developed and modified by his own culture—is said to have a character. One whose desires and impulses are not his own, has no character, no more than a steam-engine has a character.

prompt: Which of your desires are truly your own?

text: Fortune but seldom interferes with the wise man; his greatest and highest interests have been, are, and will be, directed by reason throughout the course of his life.
context: Luck affects the outer edges of a life. What matters most is guided by our own reasoning.

text: In them I seemed to draw from a source of inward joy, of sympathetic and imaginative pleasure, which could be shared in by all human beings.

text: Since it is possible that you may depart from life this very moment, regulate every act and thought accordingly.

text: A man must first appreciate the importance of what we call duty, the authority of the moral law, and the immediate dignity which the following of it gives to the person in his own eyes.

text: Few human creatures would consent to be changed into any of the lower animals, for a promise of the fullest allowance of a beast's pleasures.

text: Unlimited time and limited time afford an equal amount of pleasure, if we measure the limits of that pleasure by reason.

text: Put the case that the mind of that philanthropist were clouded by sorrow of his own, extinguishing all sympathy with the lot of others, and that, while he still has the power to benefit others in distress, he is not touched by their trouble because he is absorbed with his own; and now suppose that he tears himself out of this dead insensibility, and performs the action without any inclination to it, but simply from duty, then first has his action its genuine moral worth.

prompt: What understanding is already in you, waiting to be turned toward?

prompt: Which of your struggles is for something you don't really need?

text: For love, as an affection, cannot be commanded, but beneficence for duty's sake may; even though we are not impelled to it by any inclination- nay, are even repelled by a natural and unconquerable aversion. prompt: What would you never do because of your own sense of dignity?

text: What is a poet? A poet is an unhappy creature; his heart is torn by secret sufferings, but his lips are so formed that when the cries and the sighs escape them, they create a sound of beautiful music.

prompt: Whose cheerful surface might be hiding something you haven't asked about?

prompt: Which desire would cost you nothing to give up?

prompt: What activity makes you feel most yourself?

text: The maintenance of a due balance among the faculties now seemed to be of primary importance. The cultivation of the feelings became one of the cardinal points in my ethical and philosophical creed.

prompt: Which side of you, thinking or feeling, needs more attention?

text: If we look closer at them we everywhere come upon the dear self which is always prominent, and it is this they have in view and not the strict command of duty which would often require self-denial.

prompt: Where is the dear self hiding in your good deeds?

text: Many are the things on which we should place no reliance; for it is because he had had such complete confidence in them that a foolish man feels angry and resentful (when they fail him). context: The priestess Diotima teaches Socrates that love climbs from beautiful bodies to beautiful souls, ideas, and finally beauty itself.

prompt: Who has acted on how things seemed to them, and can you see it from there?

prompt: Which principle do you choose to live by?

prompt: What are you reaching for that you don't yet have?

text:

text:
The man who sickens of his home goes out,
Forth from his splendid halls, and straight—returns,
Feeling i'faith no better off abroad.

To hurry help to a house afire.—At once
He yawns, as soon as foot has touched the threshold,
Or drowsily goes off in sleep and seeks
Forgetfulness, or maybe bustles about

text: When an upright man is in the greatest distress, which he might have avoided if he could only have disregarded duty, is he not sustained by the consciousness that he has maintained humanity in its proper dignity in his own person and honoured it, that he has no reason to be ashamed of himself in his own sight, or to dread the inward glance of self-examination?
